question: According to the manual, what bad effects can overloading have on a commercial motor vehicle?
choice_a: It can affect steering, braking, and speed control; overloaded trucks must go slowly on upgrades but may gain too much speed on downgrades; stopping distance increases; and brakes can fail when forced to work too hard
choice_b: It only shortens tire tread life, with no other effects
choice_c: It has no effect as long as the driver compensates by driving faster
choice_d: It only affects the vehicle's fuel economy
explanation: The manual states overloading can affect steering, braking, and speed control; overloaded trucks must go slowly on upgrades but may gain too much speed on downgrades; stopping distance increases; and brakes can fail when forced to work too hard.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.2.2 Legal Weight Limits

question: When does the manual warn that it may not be safe to operate a vehicle at the legal maximum weight?
choice_a: Only when crossing a state line
choice_b: During bad weather or in mountains
choice_c: Only when hauling livestock
choice_d: Legal maximum weight is always safe regardless of conditions
explanation: The manual warns that during bad weather or in mountains, it may not be safe to operate at legal maximum weights, and drivers should take this into account before driving.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.2.2 Legal Weight Limits

question: Why is a high center of gravity especially dangerous, according to the manual?
choice_a: It only affects fuel economy
choice_b: It reduces stopping distance
choice_c: It makes a vehicle more likely to tip over, and this is most dangerous in curves or when the driver has to swerve to avoid a hazard
choice_d: It has no real effect on handling
explanation: The manual states a high center of gravity (cargo piled up high or heavy cargo on top) means you are more likely to tip over, and this is most dangerous in curves or if you have to swerve to avoid a hazard.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.2.3 Don't Be Top-heavy

question: What can too much weight on the steering axle cause, per the manual?
choice_a: Improved fuel economy
choice_b: Better traction in bad weather
choice_c: No noticeable handling effect
choice_d: Hard steering, and it can damage the steering axle and tires
explanation: The manual states too much weight on the steering axle can cause hard steering and can damage the steering axle and tires.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.2.4 Balance the Weight

question: What happens when weight shifts too far to the rear, under-loading the front axle?
choice_a: It can make the steering axle weight too light to steer safely
choice_b: It improves braking performance
choice_c: It has no effect on steering
choice_d: It automatically overloads the drive axles beyond legal limits
explanation: The manual explains that under-loaded front axles, caused by shifting weight too far to the rear, can make the steering axle weight too light to steer safely.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.2.4 Balance the Weight

question: What problem can too little weight on the driving axles cause, especially in bad weather?
choice_a: The parking brake fails to engage
choice_b: Poor traction, with the drive wheels spinning easily, so the truck may not be able to keep going in bad weather
choice_c: The vehicle becomes impossible to steer
choice_d: It has no practical effect on driving
explanation: The manual states too little weight on the driving axles can cause poor traction, the drive wheels may spin easily, and during bad weather the truck may not be able to keep going.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.2.4 Balance the Weight

question: How does the manual define blocking, as used to secure cargo?
choice_a: A tarp used to protect cargo from weather
choice_b: A permit required for oversized loads
choice_c: Material shaped to fit snugly against the cargo at the front, back, and/or sides, and secured to the cargo deck to prevent movement
choice_d: A strap running from the top of the cargo to the floor or walls
explanation: The manual defines blocking as being used at the front, back, and/or sides of a piece of cargo to keep it from sliding; it is shaped to fit snugly against the cargo and secured to the cargo deck to prevent movement.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.3.1 Blocking and Bracing

question: How does bracing, as described in the manual, differ from blocking?
choice_a: Bracing and blocking are simply two names for the same device
choice_b: Bracing is only used for hanging meat loads
choice_c: Bracing is a type of tarp while blocking is a type of chain
choice_d: Bracing goes from the upper part of the cargo to the floor and/or walls of the cargo compartment to prevent movement, while blocking fits snugly against the cargo at the front, back, and/or sides
explanation: The manual states bracing is also used to prevent movement of cargo and goes from the upper part of the cargo to the floor and/or walls of the cargo compartment, distinct from blocking which is placed at the front, back, or sides of the cargo.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.3.1 Blocking and Bracing

question: On flatbed trailers or trailers without sides, what does the manual require to keep cargo from shifting or falling off?
choice_a: Cargo must be secured with tie-downs of the proper type and strength
choice_b: Cargo needs no securement if it is heavy enough
choice_c: Only a tarp is required
choice_d: Cargo may be placed loose as long as it stays under the legal weight limit
explanation: The manual states that on flatbed trailers or trailers without sides, cargo must be secured to keep it from shifting or falling off, using tie-downs of the proper type and strength.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.3.2 Cargo Tie-down

question: Why can tie-downs still be important in closed vans, even though the cargo is enclosed?
choice_a: They are required only to satisfy insurance paperwork
choice_b: They can prevent cargo shifting that may affect the handling of the vehicle
choice_c: They are purely decorative and serve no safety function
choice_d: Closed vans are exempt from all securement requirements, so tie-downs are optional
explanation: The manual notes that in closed vans, tie-downs can also be important to prevent cargo shifting that may affect the handling of the vehicle.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.3.2 Cargo Tie-down

question: Under the federal regulations described in the manual, the aggregate working load limit of a securement system must be at least what fraction of the weight of the article or group of articles it secures?
choice_a: One-quarter
choice_b: Equal to twice the weight
choice_c: One-half
choice_d: There is no minimum requirement
explanation: The manual states federal regulations require the aggregate working load limit of any securement system used to secure an article or group of articles against movement to be at least one-half times the weight of the article or group of articles.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.3.2 Cargo Tie-down

question: What types of tie-down equipment does the manual mention, and how must they be attached to the vehicle?
choice_a: Only bungee cords, attached with tape
choice_b: Duct tape and zip ties, attached anywhere convenient
choice_c: Only steel cable, with no tensioning devices
choice_d: Ropes, straps, chains, and tensioning devices such as winches, ratchets, and clinching components, attached correctly via hooks, bolts, rails, or rings
explanation: The manual states proper tie-down equipment must be used, including ropes, straps, chains, and tensioning devices (winches, ratchets, clinching components), and must be attached to the vehicle correctly using hooks, bolts, rails, or rings.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.3.2 Cargo Tie-down

question: What is the general rule for the minimum number of tie-downs cargo needs, according to the manual?
choice_a: At least one tie-down for each ten feet of cargo, with a minimum of two tie-downs no matter how small the cargo
choice_b: Exactly one tie-down regardless of cargo length
choice_c: As many tie-downs as the driver personally feels are needed, with no set minimum
choice_d: One tie-down for each twenty-five feet of cargo, with no overall minimum
explanation: The manual states cargo should have at least one tie-down for each ten feet of cargo, and no matter how small the cargo, it should have at least two tie-downs.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.3.2 Cargo Tie-down

question: What is the purpose of front-end header boards, also called "headache racks"?
choice_a: To display required safety placards
choice_b: To protect the driver from the cargo in case of a crash or emergency stop, by blocking forward movement of the cargo
choice_c: To improve the vehicle's aerodynamics
choice_d: To hold a tarp in place over open cargo
explanation: The manual states front-end header boards (headache racks) protect the driver from the cargo in case of a crash or emergency stop, and the front-end structure should block the forward movement of any cargo carried.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.3.3 Header Boards

question: What are the two basic reasons for covering cargo, according to the manual?
choice_a: To hide the cargo from view and lower insurance costs
choice_b: To satisfy a federal rule that has no real safety benefit
choice_c: To protect people from spilled cargo and to protect the cargo from weather
choice_d: To improve fuel economy and reduce road noise
explanation: The manual lists two basic reasons for covering cargo: to protect people from spilled cargo, and to protect the cargo from weather.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.3.4 Covering Cargo

question: Why should a driver look at the cargo covers in the mirrors from time to time while driving?
choice_a: To check the cover's color for nighttime visibility only
choice_b: Mirror checks of the cover are required only at fuel stops
choice_c: Cargo covers never need to be checked once secured at the start of a trip
choice_d: A flapping cover can tear loose, uncovering the cargo and possibly blocking the driver's view or someone else's
explanation: The manual advises looking at cargo covers in the mirrors from time to time while driving because a flapping cover can tear loose, uncovering the cargo and possibly blocking your view or someone else's.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.3.4 Covering Cargo

question: Since a driver cannot inspect a sealed load directly, what must the driver still check?
choice_a: That the load does not exceed gross weight and axle weight limits
choice_b: Only the seal's expiration date
choice_c: Nothing, since sealed loads are exempt from all weight rules
choice_d: That the shipper's insurance policy is current
explanation: The manual states you cannot inspect sealed loads, but you should check that you don't exceed gross weight and axle weight limits.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.3.5 Sealed and Containerized Loads

question: What does the manual say about containerized loads and how they are secured?
choice_a: Containerized loads are exempt from securement requirements because the container is sealed
choice_b: Some containers have their own tie-down devices or locks that attach to a special frame, others must be loaded onto flatbed trailers, and all must be properly secured just like any other cargo
choice_c: Containerized loads are always carried in enclosed vans, never on flatbeds
choice_d: Containerized loads only need to be secured if they will be inspected at a scale
explanation: The manual explains that some containers have their own tiedown devices or locks that attach directly to a special frame, others have to be loaded onto flatbed trailers, and they must be properly secured just like any other cargo.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.3.5 Sealed and Containerized Loads

question: Why do dry bulk tanks require special care while driving, per the manual?
choice_a: Because they are always overweight by law
choice_b: Because they cannot legally be fitted with tie-downs
choice_c: Because they have a high center of gravity and the load can shift, requiring extreme caution on curves and sharp turns
choice_d: Because they require a driver endorsement not covered in this manual
explanation: The manual states dry bulk tanks require special care because they have a high center of gravity and the load can shift, so drivers should be extremely cautious going around curves and making sharp turns.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.4.1 Dry Bulk

question: What makes hanging meat (suspended beef, pork, lamb) in a refrigerated truck a particularly unstable load?
choice_a: It is unusually lightweight and shifts in the wind
choice_b: It must always be carried on a flatbed trailer
choice_c: It has no special handling considerations compared to other freight
choice_d: It has a high center of gravity, requiring particular caution and slow speeds on sharp curves such as off ramps and on ramps
explanation: The manual states hanging meat can be a very unstable load with a high center of gravity, and particular caution is needed on sharp curves such as off ramps and on ramps, going slowly.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.4.2 Hanging Meat

question: Even when livestock are bunched together with false bulkheads, why is special care still needed on curves?
choice_a: Livestock can lean on curves, which shifts the center of gravity and makes rollover more likely
choice_b: Bunched livestock automatically stabilize the trailer with no risk
choice_c: Livestock always lie down on curves, eliminating any risk
choice_d: Curves have no effect on livestock loads
explanation: The manual notes that even when bunched, special care is necessary because livestock can lean on curves, which shifts the center of gravity and makes rollover more likely.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.4.3 Livestock

question: What does the manual say is generally required for over-length, over-width, and/or overweight (oversized) loads?
choice_a: Nothing beyond a valid commercial driver license
choice_b: Special transit permits, with driving usually limited to certain times and possibly special equipment such as wide-load signs, flashing lights, flags, or a police escort or pilot vehicles
choice_c: A note in the driver's trip log, with no permit needed
choice_d: A reduction in the tire load rating printed on the tire sidewall
explanation: The manual states over-length, over-width, and/or overweight loads require special transit permits, driving is usually limited to certain times, special equipment such as wide load signs and flashing lights may be necessary, and such loads may require a police escort or pilot vehicles bearing warning signs and/or flashing lights.
source_note: New Mexico CDL Manual, Section 3 - Transporting Cargo Safely, 3.4.4 Oversized Loads
